rows.title: The devices — Rules
rows.summary: 1. One backend, several fronts.
body: 1. **One backend, several fronts.** Flutter, the browser, CDP, emulation, input, frames and hot reload are
`backend.rs`; a front (window, terminal) only shows the screen and sends input back (ADR-devices-0001).
2. **Nothing stays alive when a device ends**: neither `flutter run` nor the browser, whether the window is
closed, `q` is pressed or the terminal hangs up. The terminal's raw mode is restored also on a panic.
3. **`render.rs` is pure** (no I/O) and tested; what depends on the operating system is only in `system.rs`.
4. **The presets are the same list as the editor's panel** (`presets.rs` and `extensions/tools/nuclear-device-manager/src/mobile-device.ts`): a
device added to one is added to the other.
5. **A device is Flutter web**: no native plugins, no `dart:io`. It is not a replacement for a real phone.
6. What a user reads is the "Synapsis devices" part of the `nuclear` CLI section (§11) of
`nuclearlang/dialects/dart/docs/07-reference/flutter.md`: a new device, key or render updates it.

body: - **`backend.rs`**: `flutter run -d chrome` with `--web-launch-url` to an empty 404 page marked
`__synapsis_device_<n>_<pid>__` (the window is named so on Wayland, and the mark names the processes); the CDP
connection to that page; `emulate` (size, density, touch, orientation, user agent of `presets.rs`); `open_app`;
input (`touch`, `wheel`, `insert_text`, `key`, `back`); `text_layer` (`__synapsisTextLayer` of the `synapsis`
package, in debug); `typing`, `screenshot`, `start_frames` (a PNG screencast), `reload` (the terminal device:
`flutter run --machine`, `app.restart`), `close` (`Browser.close` + `kill_tree`).
- **`cdp.rs`**: a minimal Chrome DevTools Protocol client. One thread owns the WebSocket (tungstenite is not
split): `call` waits for the answer, events go to a channel; `http_get` reads by Content-Length, because Chrome
keeps the connection open.
- **`presets.rs`**: the devices a device can be, the sizes of the browsers' device toolbar in CSS pixels, portrait:
`pixel7` (the default), `iphone14pro`, `iphonese`, `iphone15promax`, `galaxys20`, `galaxya51`, `ipadmini`,
`ipadair`, `ipadpro`, `tabs7`, `responsive`, `laptop`, `desktop`; each with its density, its system (iOS,
Android, web) and its identity (user agent and `navigator.platform`; none for web). Found by id or name, ignoring
case, spaces and dashes.

rows.title: The Synapsis devices
rows.summary: A Synapsis device runs a mobile app with the size, density, touch and identity of a phone or a tablet, without an emulator.
body: A Synapsis device runs a mobile app with the size, density, touch and identity of a phone or a tablet, without an
emulator. The app runs as Flutter web in a Chromium browser, and the device is emulated and driven over the Chrome
DevTools Protocol (CDP). From the command line a device is:
- **a window of its own** (`nuclear device`), like an emulator;
- **the terminal device** (`nuclear terminal-device`), the device's screen inside your terminal.
Both run inside a mobile project (a folder with `config.nuc`), build the app first, and can run several at once:
device 1, 2, 3. When a device ends, nothing stays alive: neither `flutter run` nor the browser.
A device is Flutter web: no native plugins, no `dart:io`. It is a fast test device, not a replacement for a real
phone. Why it is built this way: [ADR-devices-0001](../03-adr/0001-a-device-is-the-app-as-flutter-web-in-chromium-driven-over-cdp.md).

| `text` | colored blocks (two pixels per cell) with the app's texts written as letters in their place, readable at any size: what GNOME Terminal, XFCE, LXQt, Alacritty, Terminal.app, the Linux console, Zed and VS Code get |

Arrows, Enter and Tab go to the app. With a text field focused, keys are text (pasting too) and the commands go

- `release/stage.sh`: assembles an installation in a folder: the layout the binaries expect. Used by `install.sh`
and `package.sh`.
- `release/version.sh`: the one version of the platform, written into every manifest and lock file and checked
(the CI, the release's job `snapshot`).
- `release/package.sh`: the release archive of one target. `release/build-runtimes.sh`: what must be built before.

rows.summary: 1. One layout, one script.
body: 1. **One layout, one script.** An installation is what `release/stage.sh` assembles, from source or from an
archive; a new file an installed binary needs is added there, never in one installer only.
2. **No sudo, no administrator**: everything goes into the user's folders, and the public installers' `--uninstall`
removes everything an install created, the AI set-up's models, Ollama when it installed it, the data and the
caches included; what was on the machine before stays (ADR-installer-0005). The source installer's `--uninstall`
(a developer's machine) keeps the data.

(ADR-platform-0013); the required services' archive comes with the install (ADR-installer-0002, ADR-installer-0006).

mirror ([the runbook](docs/06-runbooks/release.md)).
5. **`docs/08-guides/ai-setup.md` is held to the profiles by a test** (`extensions/tools/nuclear-builder/tests/test_setup.nuc`
against `setup.json`): what the profile `remote` says of itself is changed in the data, then in the guide.
6. **The user runs the installed binaries**: after a change to a binary, a dialect, a platform, a runtime package
or the skill, `installer/install.sh` again.

rows.summary: The same steps run in the three.
body: | Where | How |
| The installer | `curl -fsSL https://nuclearlang.github.io/install.sh \| sh` runs it at its end, with no question |
| VS Code | the offer the first time the extension starts, or *Nuclear: Set Up the AI Services* in the command palette, or *Set-up…* in *Settings and integrations* (`Ctrl+Alt+S`) |
| A terminal, any time | `nuclear-builder setup --profile remote --yes` |
The same steps run in the three. Run it again at any time: what is installed is kept.

rows.title: Set up the AI services — 2. The steps
rows.summary: 1. What it needs.
body: 1. **What it needs.** NuclearLang (the `nuclear` command, the code of the services); from the source tree also
[uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) (the Python environments of the services). A release's archive brings its own
Python: nothing else is needed.
2. **What was local.** On a machine an earlier version set up with a local profile, a first step takes away what
NuclearLang put there for the local models: the Nuclear Developer's service and launcher, the models NuclearLang
downloaded, and Ollama when NuclearLang installed it (what was on the machine before stays, ADR-installer-0005).
`ai.env` becomes `remote`, and the step says what it removed and how many GB were freed.
3. **Install.** The Smart Graph and the MCP server, the MCP server added to every AI client on this machine
(Claude Code, Codex, Grok Build, Cursor, OpenCode, Gemini CLI: an agent opened in any of them finds Nuclear with no
step of yours), the graph's model, the knowledge base loaded into the graph (a few seconds with the vectors the
release computed; about ten minutes on a processor when they cannot be downloaded; an update whose knowledge base
did not change keeps the vectors already here, checked against the release's SHA-256, and downloads nothing), and the Smart Graph and Nuclear
Chat started. A step that fails says why and is tried again from there.

rows.title: Set up the AI services — 3. The profile
rows.summary: The Smart Graph's model is EmbeddingGemma in ONNX (0.3 GB, counted above), which makes the graph's vectors: the graph runs it itself, inside its own process, so it needs no Ollama.
body: | Profile | Models | Downloads | Memory | Measured |
| `remote` | none (the Smart Graph's own) | 0.3 GB | 2 GB | only the Smart Graph and Nuclear Chat run on this machine |
The Smart Graph's model is EmbeddingGemma in ONNX (0.3 GB, counted above), which makes the graph's vectors: the graph
runs it itself, inside its own process, so it needs no Ollama.
**`remote`: Remote agents and the Smart Graph.**
- Works: the generators (a resource, a use case, a screen) from your agent.
- Works: the compiler's checks and fixes, the documentation of every kind and decorator.
- Works: nuclear build, test and migrate from your agent.
- Works: the Smart Graph: the strategy of each request and the search of the knowledge base, for your agent.
- Works: Nuclear Builder and Nuclear Atlas in the editor, worked by the agents and API providers you choose, in Nuclear Chat.
- Does not, or less: your agent writes every line the generators do not: all of it is paid tokens.
- Does not, or less: the local models are on standby (ADR-platform-0013): nothing is answered by a model of this machine but the Smart Graph's own.

rows.summary: out).
body: - **Update:** run the installer again, or `nuclear update` (in a terminal `nuclear` also asks when a new release is
out). It brings the new version and sets the services up again with the profile `remote`, without questions; a
machine that had a local profile loses what NuclearLang put there for it (step 2 above).
- **A client installed later** (Claude Code, Codex, Grok Build, Cursor, OpenCode, Gemini CLI): `nuclear-builder setup --clients`
adds the MCP server to it.
- **Remove:** `nuclear-builder setup --remove` takes the services away, and the MCP server out of each AI client;
the graph's data stays. `--remove --all` also takes away everything the set-up installed and made: the models an
earlier version downloaded, Ollama when it installed it (on Linux it says the commands: they need your password),
the graph's and the chat's data and secrets, and its folder (Nuclear Builder's teams, keys and runs). What was on
your machine before the set-up stays. The installer's `--uninstall` runs `--remove --all`, and also takes away the
compiler's cache and the editors' extension: nothing of NuclearLang is left.
- **In a script or CI:** `--no-ai` skips the set-up, and without a terminal nothing is asked.

this way. One install runs at a time: a second one says so and stops. The set-up of the AI services runs at a low priority, so a

rows.title: `nuclear`, the command line tool — Why
rows.summary: Why
body: - One tool for a person, an agent, the editor and the MCP server: what works in one works in all.
- No need to learn every target's package manager and framework commands; `nuclear` drives them.
- It teaches: `nuclear spec --brief` for agents, `nuclear check --json` with a code and usually the exact fix.
- It never reads target code and never replaces the target's tools.

rows.summary: Claude Code runs it after each edit and gives it the tool call on stdin.
body: Claude Code runs it after each edit and gives it the tool call on stdin. When the edited file ends in `.nuc`:
- the file's project is found (`Manifest::find` over every dialect) and built with its own type definitions

rows.summary: `nuclear build` leaves the app ready to compile and repeats nothing without changes (~40 ms): 1. Creates the app if missing; syncs `config.nuc` → pubspec and loads the definitions BEFORE transpiling (packages.md).
body: `nuclear build` leaves the app ready to compile and repeats nothing without changes (~40 ms):
1. Creates the app if missing; syncs `config.nuc` → pubspec and loads the definitions BEFORE transpiling
([packages.md](packages.md)).
2. Transpiles the project; writes only what changed and deletes orphans (`.dart_tool/nuclear_files`).
3. `ensure_packages` (Synapsis's own; with `@splash` also `flutter_native_splash`, detected by the line prefix
`name:`), copies `out.copies`, `assets::write`.
4. `pub get` when `.dart_tool/package_config.json` is missing (after `flutter clean`) or the pubspec is newer than
the lock AND than `.dart_tool/nuclear_pub_get` (`pub get` does not touch an unchanged lock).
5. `build_runner --delete-conflicting-outputs` only if a file with `part` changed since
`.dart_tool/nuclear_build_runner` (`.g.dart` dates are useless: unchanged ones are not rewritten).
6. `flutter_native_splash:create` when the yaml or an image changed (`.dart_tool/nuclear_splash`). Removing `@splash`
deletes the yaml but leaves the native splash (`flutter_native_splash:remove` needs the yaml: run it by hand
first).
7. `write_line_map` → `build/app/.dart_tool/nuclear_lines.json` (`BuiltFile::lines`, for the debuggers,
`ADR-lang-0011`).

rows.summary: An agent learns Nuclear from the command, not from guessing (ADR-cli-0002): 1. Read the short sheet: `nuclear spec --brief --platform backend` (or `--dialect <name>`): only what differs from TypeScript and Dart, then the platform's brief.
body: An agent learns Nuclear from the command, not from guessing
([ADR-cli-0002](../03-adr/0002-agents-learn-nuclear-from-a-brief-a-skill-and-the-compiler.md)):
1. **Read the short sheet**: `nuclear spec --brief --platform backend` (or `--dialect <name>`): only what
differs from TypeScript and Dart, then the platform's brief.
2. **Generate before writing**: `nuclear gen` and `nuclear make` write the standard code; the agent writes by hand
only what they leave. A product is made with the tools, never by writing or porting target code by hand
([ADR-platform-0004](../../../../docs/03-adr/0004-products-are-made-with-the-tools.md)).
3. **Use a library through its definitions**: `nuclear add <package>` installs it and generates its definitions;
`nuclear defs show <Name|Name.member> --dialect <name> [--json]` prints its API, for example
`nuclear defs show FastAPI --dialect fastapi`.
4. **Check every file**: `nuclear check --json` after each change, `nuclear fix` for the exact fixes, then
`nuclear fmt`.
5. **Set the project up once**: `nuclear agent init` writes the agents' files and a hook (`nuclear agent hook`)
that checks each `.nuc` an agent edits ([what it writes](../02-architecture/agent-support.md)).

rows.summary: `nuclear` is the one command of NuclearLang.
body: `nuclear` is the one command of NuclearLang. The same binary is the compiler (`build`, `check`, `fix`, `fmt`,
`spec`, `defs`, the documentation) and the framework, Synapsis (`new`, `make`, `gen`, `run`, `test`, `install`,
`migrate`, `add`, the devices). A person, an AI agent, an editor and the MCP server all run it, so what works in
one works in all of them ([ADR-cli-0003](../03-adr/0003-one-command-nuclear.md)).
You write only `.nuc` files. `nuclear` writes the target project (Python, TypeScript or Dart) into `build/` and
runs the target's own tools there for you: you never call `pip`, `npm` or `flutter` yourself.

| `workspace rename <app> <new>` | renames the app's folder and its entry; the project's `app(name)` in its `config.nuc` stays unless `--project-name` (a project without `app(name)` takes its folder's name). Run `nuclear install` in it again: a virtual environment keeps the path it was made in |

| `workspace remove <app>` | out of the marker only; its folder stays. `--delete` deletes the folder too, never a folder outside the workspace |

Every command takes `--workspace <dir>` (default: the workspace that holds the current folder, found by walking up)
and `--json`, which prints one object, the same for every command:
```json

rows.title: The code generator — Rules
rows.summary: 1. Finished code or a refusal.
body: 1. **Finished code or a refusal.** What `gen` writes compiles as written; when it cannot write something finished
it refuses and says what to do. Never a placeholder for a model to fill (ADR-codegen-0001).
2. **The templates are the platform's data**, never code here: the Nuclear a generator writes is the same for every
dialect of a platform. This code only reads the fields, picks the templates and writes each file at the
platform's `[layout]` path.
3. **Nothing is overwritten, nothing is declared twice.** A file that exists is kept; a `merge` piece gets only the
whole members it lacks; a name another file declares stops the command before it writes.
4. **A new kind or decorator of a platform updates its generators and skeletons** in the same change; the tests
`a_generated_resource_compiles_with_every_dialect`, `every_skeleton_parses`,
`every_new_project_compiles_with_its_dialect` and `make_writes_every_kind_where_the_platform_says` hold it.
5. **A change to what a command takes or writes** updates the user guide
(`nuclear-synapsis-framework/docs/08-guides/generators.md`), `GEN_USAGE` / `USAGE`, the MCP tool of the same
name ([the MCP server](../mcp/AGENTS.md)) and the `nuclear` skill.

rows.title: The code generator
rows.summary: What `nuclear new`, `nuclear make` and `nuclear gen` write into a project.
body: What `nuclear new`, `nuclear make` and `nuclear gen` write into a project. `gen` writes finished code that compiles
from a resource's data (models, repository, a use case per action, the facade's aliases, the controller or the
screen, the tests) and wires a use case into its component. `make` writes one skeleton of a kind, to fill in; `new`
the files of a new project. A person, an AI agent, the MCP server and the Nuclear Builder all generate through it, so
a standard feature costs no model tokens.

rows.summary: (ADR-codegen-0001).
body: - **Finished code or a refusal, never a placeholder**: measured, skeletons were worse (29 of 42 against 37)

- **Fields from data**: `--fields`, `--from-json` or `--from-spec`.
- **Nothing overwritten, nothing declared twice.** Written in Rust, called by `nuclear`.

rows.title: The code generator: overview — `gen`: from a resource's data to files
rows.summary: 1. The fields (`gen_command` of the command, `generate.rs`): `nested`), a list under a key of a paged answer gives `<Name>Page`, `null` an optional field, a key that is not the field's camelCase name gets `@key` (`json_key`).
body: 1. **The fields** (`gen_command` of the command, `generate.rs`):
- `--fields "id:int name:string origin:Origin?"` → `parse_fields`.
- `--from-json <file|url>` → `from_json`: a nested object becomes a model `<Name><Key>` (`object_model`,
`nested`), a list under a key of a paged answer gives `<Name>Page`, `null` an optional field, a key that is not
the field's camelCase name gets `@key` (`json_key`). A url is fetched with `curl` (`fetch_text`) and also gives
the API's base and path.
- `--from-spec <spec.md>` → its example answer (`spec_json`), else its `Key | Type | Description` table
(`from_spec`); a table with objects it does not detail reads the API's answer from the spec's `GET <url>` line
(`spec_url`).
2. **The checks, before anything is written**: every type a field names is basic (`BASIC`), a model of the same
answer or declared in the project (`nuclear_transpile::map::inventory`); a database resource takes only columns
of basic types (a relation is written by hand) and has no generated `search` (which column is searched is a
decision); the actions are of `ACTIONS`; the platform has pieces for the source (`when = "rest"` / `"db"`:
mobile and web read APIs, a database resource is backend only); a name another file declares is refused (N0303).

rows.title: The code generator: overview — `gen`: from a resource's data to files
rows.summary: 3. The context (`context(&Resource)`, `usecase_context(&UseCase)`): the values the templates read.
body: 3. **The context** (`context(&Resource)`, `usecase_context(&UseCase)`): the values the templates read. `Name`/`name`,
`Names`/`names` (`plural`, or `--plural`), `component`/`Component`, `fields`, `data` (the fields without the
key), `models`, `rest`/`db`, `path`, `baseUrl`, `connection`, `paged`, `Page`, `items`, `idType`,
`actions.<action>`, `each_action`, `screen`/`Screen`, and the samples the tests use (`sample_of`, `sample`). The
whole list is in `nuclearlang/docs/07-reference/dialects.md`.
4. **The plan** (`plan(dialect, what, ctx)`): for each `[[generators.<what>]]` piece of the platform, skipped when
its `when` value is not true, once per item of its `each` list: the declaration's name (`name` rendered), its
path (the `[layout]` place of its `kind` with `{component}`, `{screen}`, `{file}` = the name in snake_case), and
its text (`template` rendered, then put in the canonical layout by `nuclear_syntax::fmt::format`).
5. **The write** (`write`): a missing file is `created`; a file that exists is `kept`; a `merge = true` piece (a
facade, a repository, a controller) gets the members it lacks, each one whole (`members`: its decorators, its
head line and its body, told by the head line), and says `added to`. `--dry-run` shows the plan and writes
nothing. A component that does not exist is created first (`generators.component`).

rows.title: The code generator: overview — `gen`: from a resource's data to files
rows.summary: 6. The `Http` connection (`ensure_http`): a REST resource whose base url no connection of the app's `appConfig` file has gets one written with the platform's `[gen] http` form, or `http_named` (named after the component) when the app already has another; the repository then names it.
body: 6. **The `Http` connection** (`ensure_http`): a REST resource whose base url no connection of the app's
`appConfig` file has gets one written with the platform's `[gen] http` form, or `http_named` (named after the
component) when the app already has another; the repository then names it.
`gen usecase` (`UseCase`, `Route`, `parse_route`, `result_parts`): the signature of `exec` is read from the project
with `nuclear_transpile::map::shape`, never typed again. `--calls <Repository>.<method>` writes the use case too
(a method that answers no `Result` goes inside an `Ok`); `--route "<VERB> <prefix>[/<path>]"` adds its route to the
controller of the prefix, made when missing (a `{name}` of the path must be a parameter of the use case; the route
calls it with `~` only when `exec` awaits). A use case that is neither declared nor given `--calls` is refused with
the place and the form to write it.
`gen inspect` prints what the project has as JSON: its platform and dialect, its components with their declarations
(`kind`, `name`, `file`), what is outside a component, and the generators of its platform.

rows.title: The code generator: overview
rows.summary: The crate `nuclear-codegen` writes files into a project for three commands.
body: The crate `nuclear-codegen` writes files into a project for three commands. `nuclear gen` writes finished code
from data; `nuclear make` writes a skeleton of one kind; `nuclear new` the files of a new project. The crate writes
and reports `(Wrote::Created | Kept, path)`; the command (`tools/cli/src/framework/mod.rs`) parses and prints. Both write Nuclear only, and neither overwrites a file. What a user types and gets is in
[the generators' guide](../../../../nuclear-synapsis-framework/docs/08-guides/generators.md).

rows.summary: `generate_screen` and `api_inspect` run these commands (the MCP server).
body: - A person or an agent in a shell: `nuclear gen`, `nuclear make` ([the CLI](../../../cli/AGENTS.md)).
- The MCP server: `project_inspect`, `generate_component`, `generate_resource`, `generate_usecase`,
`generate_screen` and `api_inspect` run these commands ([the MCP server](../../../mcp/AGENTS.md)).
- The Nuclear Builder's *Generate* stage: `nuclear gen resource` for each resource a spec names, before any agent works
([the Nuclear Builder](../../../../extensions/tools/nuclear-builder/AGENTS.md)).
The state manager that `make screen` (and `make statemanager`) writes loads `Ok([])`: it calls no use case,
because a component made by `gen resource` has none of the skeleton's (`hello` exists only in a component made by
`make component`). The user replaces it with a call to one of the component's aliases.

rows.title: The generators: `nuclear new`, `gen` and `make` — `nuclear gen resource <component> <Name>`
rows.summary: A resource is something the app lists, reads and changes.
body: A resource is something the app lists, reads and changes. The fields come from one of three sources:
```sh
nuclear gen resource books Book --fields "id:int title:string author:string?"
nuclear gen resource users User --from-json users.json          # an example answer of an API (a file or a url)
nuclear gen resource episodes Episode --from-spec episodes.md    # the spec's Key | Type | Description table
From `--from-spec`, a `GET https://...` line gives the API, and a snake_case key keeps its name with `@key`:
The other options:
| Option | Meaning |
| `--source rest:<base url>` \| `rest` \| `db` | another API (an HTTP repository) or the database (default: `db`; `rest` with a url). The web platform has no `db` |
| `--actions list,get,search,create,update,delete` | one use case each. Default: `list,get` for `rest`, every one for `db` |
| `--path <path>` | the API's path of the resource (default: the url's last segment, or the name) |
| `--screen <screen>` | mobile and web: a screen that lists the resource |
| `--plural <Names>` | when the English plural is not the right one |
| `--dry-run` | print the files and their code, write nothing |
What it writes, per platform (from `--dry-run`):

rows.title: The generators: `nuclear new`, `gen` and `make`
rows.summary: Most of an app is standard code: an entity, a repository, a use case that only calls it, a controller, a screen that lists a resource, their tests.
body: Most of an app is standard code: an entity, a repository, a use case that only calls it, a controller, a screen
that lists a resource, their tests. In NuclearLang that code is written by a tool, not by a person and not by a
model: the result is the same every time, it compiles as written, and it costs no model tokens. A person, an AI
agent, the MCP server and the Nuclear Builder all call the same generators.
This is how products are made on the platform: `nuclear new`, `nuclear gen` and `nuclear make` come first, and only
what they leave is written by hand, in Nuclear
([ADR-platform-0004](../../../../docs/03-adr/0004-products-are-made-with-the-tools.md),
[ADR-codegen-0001](../03-adr/0001-the-generators-write-finished-code-the-agent-only-what-is-not-standard.md)).
The three commands:
| Command | Writes |
| `nuclear new <name> -p <platform>` | the files of a new project |
| `nuclear gen resource` / `gen usecase` / `gen component` | finished code that compiles, or a refusal that says what to do |
| `nuclear make <kind> <component> <Name>` (`nuclear g`) | one skeleton of a kind, to fill in |

rows.title: The context documents of a project — The rules
rows.summary: The rules
rows.body: - Never overwrite a document that exists: merge what is missing into it.

rows.title: The context documents of a project — The rules
rows.summary: `06-runbooks`.
body: - **State** (how the system is today): `00-context`, `01-product`, `02-architecture`, `05-standards`,
`06-runbooks`. Kept true: a change that makes one of them wrong updates it in the same change.
- **Decisions** (why it is so): `03-adr`, MADR format. An accepted ADR is never edited: a new ADR replaces it and the
old one is marked `superseded by ADR-XXXX`.
- **Changes** (what is being built): `04-specs/NNN-feature/` with `requirements.md` (what and why),
`design.md` (how) and `tasks.md` (small, verifiable tasks); life cycle `draft → approved → in-progress → done`,
listed in `04-specs/README.md`. This is how spec-driven development works (as in Spec Kit and OpenSpec): the
spec of a change is written and reviewed before its code, and the state documents are the current truth.
- The prefixes `00-` … `06-` only fix the reading order, from the general to the concrete.
- Acceptance criteria are written in **EARS**: `WHEN <trigger> THE SYSTEM SHALL <response>`,
`IF <unwanted condition> THEN THE SYSTEM SHALL <response>`, `WHILE <state> ...`, `WHERE <feature> ...`.
- Every document starts with the frontmatter `status`, `owner`, `updated` (YYYY-MM-DD), `related`.
- Short files, one subject each. A document that grows past a few hundred lines is split by subject.
- Never invent: what cannot be read from the code or the user's words is a `TODO(user): <concrete question>`.

rows.title: The context documents of a project — What a Nuclear project adds
rows.summary: Nuclear (the MCP server's `nuclear_start`) and checks its work.
body: - `AGENTS.md` ends with a section between `<!-- nuclearlang -->` and `<!-- /nuclearlang -->`: how an agent learns
Nuclear (the MCP server's `nuclear_start`) and checks its work. `nuclear agent init` refreshes only that section.
- `02-architecture/overview.md` holds the platform's layout: where each kind of piece goes. The meaning of each
kind is the platform's topic (`nuclear help <platform>`), never copied into the project: it always comes from the
installed version.
- `02-architecture/dependencies.md`: the libraries are in `config.nuc` (`nuclear add <package>`).
